newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels fire shots in memory of dead comrades.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels fire shots in memory of dead comrades.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 VIPs at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima fired six shots into the air early on Tuesday and shouted defiant slogans in memory of comrades whose deaths led to the formation of their movement.
Television images showed at least one flash from gunfire at the front of the diplomatic compound and the sound of six shots fired at roughly two-second intervals.
Between the detonations a male voice could be heard shouting the names of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels' dead comrades.
The gunshots, fired shortly before dawn, were immediately followed by a defiant speech broadcast via megaphone from inside the residence, witnesses said.

The five-minute speech, apparently made by one of the 15 guerrillas holed up in the residence for 49 days, made reference to a textile factory labour dispute in which the leader of the hostage-takers participated 18 years ago.
"Today, February 4, 1997, we pay homage to the comrade workers" who died in the strike at the Cromotex factory near Lima in 1979, the unidentified rebel shouted.
"Comrades, take our blood and transform it into the torrent of revolutionary force," the rebel shouted at the end of his speech. "Did you hear that?" he added.

Witnesses said police on guard around the building did not appear alarmed by the shots or the rebels' shouts, although an armoured vehicle parked about 200 yards (200 meters) from the residence started its engine. The vehicle did not move and the engine was turned off after about 20 minutes.
A policeman on duty about a block from the residence said the rebels fired the shots as a reminder of their presence.
"They (the rebels) are just trying to grab our attention," said the police officer, who asked not to be named.

Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, the MRTA leader who led the spectacular Dec. 17 assault on a cocktail party at the residence, took part in the Cromotex dispute and has named the operation after Hemegidio Huertas, one of six workers to die in clashes with police during the strike.
Following the speech, the rebels placed three new signs in an upper window of the diplomatic mansion commemorating the Cromotex dispute.
One sign read: "Glory and honour to the martyr workers of Cromotex Feb. 4 1979-1997." The other signs contained the names of the workers who died in the strike.

Following the strike, Cerpa was arrested and held in jail for 10 months but after release he went underground and started to help organise the MRTA. Cerpa, 43, is now the highest-ranking MRTA leader not in jail.
The rebels, who possess AKM assault rifles and grenade launchers, have fired what police later described as warning shots into the air several times during the seven-week siege.
Tuesday's shooting was the first at the site since the guerrillas fired at police aboard a police convoy in front of the residence on Jan. 27.
The rebels remain deadlocked with the Peruvian government over their demand for the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, who returns to Lima from Washington later on Tuesday, has said freeing the MRTA prisoners was "out of the question."
But at a weekend crisis summit in Toronto with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Fujimori agreed to resume direct talks with the MRTA to end the siege peacefully.
The two sides have not held face-to-face negotiations since Dec. 28.
The guerrillas have released most of the more than 500 guests they seized when they stormed a garden party at the residence on Dec. 17.
They still hold two government ministers, police chiefs, congressmen, judges, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and Fujimori's younger brother.
